title: Introduction to Accounting
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L Introduction to Financial Accounting curriculum: nature and scope of accounting, accounting concepts and conventions, double-entry bookkeeping, books of original entry, ledgers and trial balance, cash books, bank reconciliation, correction of errors, final accounts for sole traders, depreciation, bad debts, accruals/prepayments, and stock valuation.

questions.question: Accounting is best defined as the process of identifying, measuring, and ____ economic information to permit informed judgments by users.
questions.explanation: The classic definition of accounting covers identifying, measuring, and communicating economic information to users.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary function of accounting?
options: Setting monetary policy for the economy
questions.correct_answer: Setting monetary policy for the economy
questions.explanation: Monetary policy is a macroeconomic/central bank function, not a function of accounting.

questions.question: Bookkeeping differs from accounting mainly because bookkeeping is concerned with:
questions.explanation: Bookkeeping is the mechanical, routine recording of transactions, while accounting also includes classifying, summarizing, and interpreting.

questions.question: Which branch of accounting is primarily concerned with providing information to parties outside the organization, such as shareholders and creditors?
questions.explanation: Financial accounting focuses on preparing general-purpose statements for external users.

questions.question: Which of the following is an internal user of accounting information?
questions.explanation: Management is part of the organization and uses accounting information internally for planning and control; the others are external users.

questions.question: A bank considering whether to grant a loan to a business is an example of which category of accounting information user?
questions.explanation: A bank is outside the entity and uses published accounts to assess creditworthiness, making it an external user.

questions.question: The accounting concept that states a business is treated as separate and distinct from its owner is the:
questions.explanation: The business entity concept requires that the affairs of the business be kept separate from the personal affairs of the owner.

questions.question: The concept that assumes a business will continue operating for the foreseeable future is called the:
questions.explanation: The going concern concept assumes the business will continue in operation long enough to carry out its objectives and commitments.

questions.question: Recording only transactions that can be expressed in monetary terms reflects the:
questions.explanation: The money measurement concept states that only items measurable in monetary terms are recorded in the accounts.

questions.question: Under the prudence (conservatism) concept, an accountant should:
options: anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses
recognize revenue before it is earned
questions.correct_answer: anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses
questions.explanation: Prudence requires caution so that assets and income are not overstated and liabilities and losses are not understated.

questions.question: The consistency concept in accounting requires that:
options: the same accounting methods be applied from one period to the next
all businesses use identical accounting policies
figures be rounded consistently to the nearest naira
revenue be recognized only on cash receipt
questions.correct_answer: the same accounting methods be applied from one period to the next
questions.explanation: Consistency requires a business to use the same accounting treatment for similar items period after period to allow comparability.

questions.question: The matching (accrual) concept requires that:
options: expenses be matched against the revenue they helped generate in the same period
expenses be recorded only when cash is paid
revenue be recorded only when cash is received
all costs be treated as expenses of the year in which they are paid
questions.correct_answer: expenses be matched against the revenue they helped generate in the same period
questions.explanation: The matching concept links expenses to the revenues they helped earn within the same accounting period, regardless of cash movement.

questions.question: The double-entry principle states that every transaction has:
options: a debit entry and a corresponding credit entry of equal value
two debit entries of equal value
one entry only, affecting one account
a debit entry that must exceed the credit entry
questions.correct_answer: a debit entry and a corresponding credit entry of equal value
questions.explanation: Double entry bookkeeping records each transaction twice, as a debit in one account and an equal credit in another.

questions.question: The accounting equation is correctly expressed as:
questions.explanation: The fundamental accounting equation shows that a business's resources (assets) are financed by the owner's capital and outside liabilities.

questions.question: When a business purchases equipment for cash, the effect on the accounting equation is:
options: one asset increases while another asset (cash) decreases
no effect, since it is an internal transfer
questions.correct_answer: one asset increases while another asset (cash) decreases
questions.explanation: Buying equipment for cash simply swaps one asset (cash) for another (equipment); total assets remain unchanged.

questions.question: In double-entry bookkeeping, an increase in an asset account is recorded as a:
questions.explanation: By convention, asset accounts increase on the debit side and decrease on the credit side.

questions.question: An increase in a liability account is recorded as a:
questions.explanation: Liability accounts increase on the credit side and decrease on the debit side.

questions.question: Which document is issued by a seller to a buyer requesting payment for goods supplied on credit?
questions.explanation: An invoice is a source document sent by the seller detailing goods sold and the amount owed by the buyer.
questions.topic: Source documents and books of original entry

questions.question: A credit note is issued when:
options: goods are returned by a customer or an overcharge is corrected
a customer pays cash for goods
a supplier delivers new goods on credit
questions.correct_answer: goods are returned by a customer or an overcharge is corrected
questions.explanation: A credit note reduces the amount a customer owes, typically issued for returned goods or overcharges.
questions.topic: Source documents and books of original entry

questions.question: Which book of original entry is used to record credit purchases of goods for resale?
questions.explanation: The purchases day book (purchases journal) records all credit purchases of goods intended for resale before posting to the ledger.
questions.topic: Source documents and books of original entry

questions.question: The book of original entry used to record credit sales returns from customers is the:
options: Sales returns day book (returns inwards journal)
questions.correct_answer: Sales returns day book (returns inwards journal)
questions.explanation: Goods returned by customers on credit sales are recorded first in the sales returns (returns inwards) day book.
questions.topic: Source documents and books of original entry

questions.question: Which of these transactions would be recorded in the general journal (journal proper) rather than a specialized day book?
options: Purchase of a non-current asset on credit
questions.correct_answer: Purchase of a non-current asset on credit
questions.explanation: Non-routine transactions such as the credit purchase of a fixed asset are recorded in the journal proper, not in the specialized day books used for routine trading transactions.
questions.topic: Source documents and books of original entry

questions.question: The ledger account that shows amounts owed to a business by its credit customers is called the:
questions.explanation: The debtors/receivables ledger holds individual accounts for customers who owe the business money.

questions.question: A trial balance is best described as a:
options: list of ledger account balances used to check arithmetic accuracy
formal financial statement showing profit or loss
statement of a business's assets and liabilities only
questions.correct_answer: list of ledger account balances used to check arithmetic accuracy
questions.explanation: A trial balance lists all ledger balances to confirm that total debits equal total credits before preparing final accounts.

questions.question: If a trial balance fails to balance, this indicates that:
options: at least one error affecting the equality of debits and credits has occurred
the business made a loss for the period
the balance sheet cannot ever be prepared
questions.correct_answer: at least one error affecting the equality of debits and credits has occurred
questions.explanation: An imbalance signals that a one-sided error, such as an omitted or mismatched entry, has occurred somewhere in the double entry.

questions.question: Which of the following would appear on the debit side of a trial balance?
questions.explanation: Purchases is an expense-type account with a normal debit balance, so it appears on the debit side of the trial balance.

questions.question: The process of transferring entries from the books of original entry to the ledger accounts is called:
questions.explanation: Posting is the act of transferring recorded transactions from journals/day books into the relevant ledger accounts.

questions.question: In a three-column cash book, the three columns typically represent:
questions.explanation: A three-column cash book has columns for discount allowed/received, cash transactions, and bank transactions.

questions.question: A cheque paid into the bank but not yet credited by the bank at the statement date is known as:
questions.explanation: An uncredited lodgement is money banked by the business that has not yet appeared on the bank statement.

questions.question: A cheque issued by a business but not yet presented to the bank for payment is called:
questions.explanation: An unpresented cheque has been written and recorded by the business but has not yet cleared through the banking system.

questions.question: The main purpose of a bank reconciliation statement is to:
options: explain differences between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance
calculate the profit of the business
determine the value of closing stock
questions.correct_answer: explain differences between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance
questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation identifies and explains timing differences and errors between the cash book and the bank's records.

questions.question: Bank charges shown on the bank statement but not yet in the cash book should be:
options: deducted in the cash book to update its balance
added to the bank statement balance
treated as an error requiring no adjustment
questions.correct_answer: deducted in the cash book to update its balance
questions.explanation: Since bank charges reduce the account and the business only learns of them from the statement, the cash book must be updated by deducting them.

questions.question: An error where a transaction is completely omitted from the books is called an error of:
questions.explanation: An error of omission occurs when a transaction is entirely left out of the accounting records.

questions.question: Recording a purchase of a motor vehicle as an expense in the repairs account is an example of an error of:
questions.explanation: An error of principle occurs when a transaction is recorded in a way that violates a fundamental accounting principle, such as treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure.

questions.question: A suspense account is opened when:
options: the trial balance fails to balance and the cause is not yet known
a business wants to record petty cash
a customer's account is written off as a bad debt
questions.correct_answer: the trial balance fails to balance and the cause is not yet known
questions.explanation: A suspense account temporarily holds the difference in an unbalanced trial balance until the error causing it is found and corrected.

questions.question: Which type of error does NOT cause the trial balance to disagree?
options: Error of complete reversal is the only one listed that still balances
Error of unequal debit and credit amounts
Casting error on one side only
questions.correct_answer: Error of complete reversal is the only one listed that still balances
questions.explanation: Errors of original entry, complete reversal, omission, commission, principle, and compensating errors all preserve equal debits and credits, so the trial balance still balances despite the error.

questions.question: The final account prepared to determine the gross profit of a trading business is the:
questions.explanation: The trading account matches sales revenue against the cost of goods sold to arrive at gross profit.

questions.question: Gross profit is calculated as:
options: Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold
Sales plus Cost of Goods Sold
questions.correct_answer: Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold
questions.explanation: Gross profit is the surplus of sales revenue over the direct cost of the goods sold during the period.

questions.question: Cost of Goods Sold is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold equals the stock available for sale (opening stock plus purchases) less what remains unsold (closing stock).

questions.question: Net profit is transferred from the profit and loss account to the:
questions.explanation: For a sole trader, the net profit for the period increases the owner's capital account.

questions.question: In a sole trader's balance sheet, drawings are:
options: treated as an expense in the profit and loss account
questions.explanation: Drawings represent amounts the owner has withdrawn for personal use and reduce the owner's capital in the balance sheet.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a current asset?
questions.explanation: Inventory is expected to be sold or used up within the normal operating cycle, making it a current asset, unlike the other listed items which are non-current.

questions.question: The main method of depreciating an asset by an equal amount each year over its useful life is called the:
questions.explanation: The straight-line method spreads the depreciable amount evenly across the asset's estimated useful life.

questions.question: A machine costing ₦100,000 with an estimated residual value of ₦10,000 and a useful life of 6 years will have an annual straight-line depreciation charge of:
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life = (100,000 - 10,000) / 6 = ₦15,000.

questions.question: Under the reducing (diminishing) balance method, depreciation is calculated on the:
options: net book value at the start of each year
revalued amount at the end of the asset's life
questions.correct_answer: net book value at the start of each year
questions.explanation: The reducing balance method applies a fixed percentage to the asset's carrying (net book) value, which declines each year, producing a higher charge in early years.

questions.question: Depreciation is best described as:
options: the allocation of the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
a fund set aside in cash to replace an asset
an increase in the market value of an asset
the total cost of purchasing a new asset
questions.correct_answer: the allocation of the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
questions.explanation: Depreciation systematically spreads an asset's cost as an expense over the periods that benefit from its use, matching the matching concept.

questions.question: A debt that is considered irrecoverable and is written off is called a:
questions.explanation: A bad debt is a specific debtor's balance that the business has concluded will never be collected and so writes off as an expense.

questions.question: A provision for doubtful debts is created to:
options: anticipate debtors who may fail to pay in the future
record debts already confirmed as bad
replace the need for a debtors ledger
questions.correct_answer: anticipate debtors who may fail to pay in the future
questions.explanation: In line with the prudence concept, a provision for doubtful debts estimates the portion of outstanding debtors that may not be collected.

questions.question: An increase in the provision for doubtful debts is recorded in the profit and loss account as:
options: a reduction in capital only, with no P&L effect
questions.explanation: An increase in the provision reduces profit and is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account for the period.

questions.question: Rent paid in advance at the end of an accounting period should be treated as a:
options: prepayment, shown as a current asset
accrual, shown as a current liability
questions.correct_answer: prepayment, shown as a current asset
questions.explanation: A prepayment is an amount paid in advance for a future benefit and is recognized as a current asset until the period it relates to arrives.

questions.question: An expense that has been incurred but not yet paid for at the end of the accounting period is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An accrued expense has been used up or incurred within the period but remains unpaid, and is recorded as a current liability.

questions.question: Failing to adjust for accrued expenses at year end would cause profit for the period to be:
questions.explanation: If an incurred expense is not recorded, total expenses are understated, which in turn overstates the reported profit.

questions.question: Which of the following is capital expenditure?
options: Purchase of a delivery van for the business
Payment of monthly fuel for the delivery van
questions.correct_answer: Purchase of a delivery van for the business
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure acquires or improves a non-current asset that will benefit the business over more than one accounting period.

questions.question: Treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure in the accounts will:
options: understate profit and understate non-current assets
overstate profit and overstate non-current assets
have no effect on profit or assets
questions.correct_answer: understate profit and understate non-current assets
questions.explanation: Wrongly expensing a capital item increases expenses (reducing profit) and leaves the asset out of the balance sheet, understating non-current assets.

questions.question: Carriage inwards (cost of transporting purchased goods to the business) is treated in the final accounts as:
options: part of the cost of purchases in the trading account
a selling and distribution expense in the profit and loss account
questions.correct_answer: part of the cost of purchases in the trading account
questions.explanation: Carriage inwards is added to the cost of purchases because it is a cost incurred to bring goods to a saleable condition and location.

questions.question: Carriage outwards (cost of delivering goods to customers) is treated in the final accounts as:
options: an expense in the profit and loss account
part of the cost of purchases
a deduction from gross profit before it is calculated
questions.correct_answer: an expense in the profit and loss account
questions.explanation: Carriage outwards is a distribution cost incurred after the sale and is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account, not the trading account.

questions.question: Under the FIFO (First-In-First-Out) method of stock valuation, closing stock is valued using the:
options: cost of the most recently purchased items
cost of the earliest purchased items
questions.correct_answer: cost of the most recently purchased items
questions.explanation: FIFO assumes the earliest purchased goods are sold first, so the units remaining in closing stock are valued at the most recent purchase costs.

questions.question: The Weighted Average Cost (AVCO) method of stock valuation values inventory by:
options: dividing the total cost of goods available for sale by the total units available
always using the oldest purchase price
always using the newest purchase price
using the market selling price of the goods
questions.correct_answer: dividing the total cost of goods available for sale by the total units available
questions.explanation: AVCO calculates a weighted average unit cost by dividing total cost of goods available by the total number of units available for sale.

questions.question: According to the lower of cost and net realizable value rule, inventory should be valued at:
options: whichever of cost or net realizable value is lower
always at its original purchase cost
always at its expected selling price
whichever of cost or net realizable value is higher
questions.correct_answer: whichever of cost or net realizable value is lower
questions.explanation: The prudence concept requires stock to be valued at the lower of cost and net realizable value so that inventory is not overstated.

questions.question: A business that does not maintain a complete double-entry system and instead keeps only partial records is said to use:
questions.explanation: Single entry, or incomplete records, describes a bookkeeping system that does not consistently apply double entry, common in small businesses.

questions.question: Under incomplete records, opening capital can be estimated by preparing a:
questions.explanation: A statement of affairs lists assets and liabilities to derive capital, similar to a balance sheet, when full records are not kept.

questions.question: In a not-for-profit organization's accounts, the equivalent of the profit and loss account is the:
questions.explanation: Not-for-profit organizations prepare an income and expenditure account, on the accrual basis, to determine a surplus or deficit rather than a profit.

questions.question: In a club's or society's accounts, the record of cash actually received and paid during the period is called the:
questions.explanation: The receipts and payments account is a summary of the cash book, showing actual cash received and paid during the period on a cash basis.

questions.question: In not-for-profit organization accounts, the accumulated fund is broadly equivalent to a sole trader's:
questions.explanation: The accumulated fund represents the organization's net worth built up over time, serving the same role as capital does for a sole trader.

questions.question: A control account (e.g. the sales ledger control account) is mainly used to:
options: provide a check on the arithmetic accuracy of the individual ledger
replace the need for individual customer accounts entirely
questions.correct_answer: provide a check on the arithmetic accuracy of the individual ledger
questions.explanation: A control account summarizes and cross-checks the total of individual accounts in a subsidiary ledger, helping to detect errors.

questions.question: Which item would appear on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
questions.explanation: Cash received from debtors reduces the amount owed, so it is credited to the sales ledger control account, which otherwise tracks debtor balances.

questions.question: In a manufacturing account, the cost of raw materials consumed plus direct labour and direct expenses gives the:
questions.explanation: Prime cost is the total of direct materials consumed, direct labour, and direct expenses before factory overheads are added.
